text: When someone dies, their subscriptions don't. Three million Americans die every year, and their families spend months calling companies, one at a time, death certificate in hand.

Rachel's mother, Eleanor, died last month. Rachel tells Afterword once. Gemini reads the death certificate, in English or Spanish. Eleven checks run, including image forensics, and then the image is deleted.
From Eleanor's PayPal activity, Afterword finds eight things still charging her: subscriptions, an annual renewal due in days, an unpaid invoice, and what has been taken since she died.
Here is the money over time. Grey before her death. Red after it.
One click sends a signed notice to seven companies. Each company's own agent checks it against its PayPal records, and pauses billing right away. That step can be undone.
Because a tool like this could be abused, Eleanor's own inbox is asked: was this a mistake? Nothing irreversible happens until that window closes.
Then the agents cancel and refund through the PayPal Agent Toolkit. Each company signs a receipt, and Afterword re-reads PayPal to confirm it really happened.
A year of charges that will never be taken.

Some companies review by hand. Before anyone decides, a Gemini reviewer agent investigates. It reads the notice, checks PayPal itself, and recommends. It has no tool that can move money. A person approves.
And this isn't a mock-up. The same code runs on real PayPal sandbox subscriptions, with PayPal's own IDs to prove it.
Across the network, AG Studio shows every notice, every PayPal step, and every attack that was stopped.
You can try to break it. Ten live attacks, from forged certificates to talking the AI reviewer into a refund. All ten are blocked.
And if Eleanor were alive? One click from her, and every pause is undone. No money moves, and the person who reported her is flagged.
